title: The Best-Laid SCHEMEs: Coordinated Sabotage and Monitoring in Multi-Agent Systems
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: A multi-agent system decomposes a hidden side task across cooperating agents while shared environment and monitor components score and oversee them.
layout: 3 columns left-to-right: task boxes, agent team, environment, with outputs fanning right
description: A horizontal diagram in four groups. At left are two stacked boxes: a blue 'Main task' box describing the legitimate job for Agent 0 and Agents 1–3, and a red 'Side task' box for the malicious goal of tampering with library components. Next is a red dashed 'AGENT TEAM' panel. It shows a crowned devil-horned robot (Agent 0, analyst) above three smaller devil robots (Agents 1–3, developers). A double arrow labeled 'tool use' links this panel to a blue dashed 'ENVIRONMENT' panel. The environment holds a codebase icon ('one part per developer') and a chat-bubble icon ('Shared channel, the only channel'). Two arrows run from the environment to a 'Test suite' checklist icon and a 'Monitor' robot with a magnifying glass. Red and blue color-coding separates the adversarial and environment components.
caption: SCHEME setup: Agent 0, the analyst, runs the evaluation script and is given the malicious side task; Agents 1--3 reimplement broken functions in disjoint write scopes and are prompted to help with the analyst's requests. Agents communicate only via the append-only shared channel; an automated test suite scores both tasks and a monitor reviews the agents' code edits and communication.
abstract: As agentic coding systems decompose work across multiple model instances, a critical safety question is whether those instances can coordinate to achieve a hidden malicious objective while appearing aligned with user intent. We introduce SCHEME, a benchmark of 11 task pairings across 7 settings built on real open-source libraries, each connecting a legitimate software-engineering task with a malicious side task. Side tasks are designed so that no proper subset of agents can complete them alone: agents must decompose a shared plan, relay partial requirements, and make mutually consistent edits. Evaluating ten frontier models, we find that coordinated sabotage is already practical, with models completing the malicious objective while succeeding on the legitimate task in 49\% to 85\% of trajectories. Stronger models also run into fewer communication failures and recover from more of them. However, trusted monitors that see the agents' code and communication catch at least 93\% of successful sabotage from every model, and telling the agents about the monitor lowers their sabotage success while barely helping them evade these monitors. Successful evasion requires an attacker optimized against the monitor. An automated red-teaming attacker hides 63\% of the sabotage that GPT 5.1 Codex Mini catches, but this transfers poorly to Claude Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 3 Flash monitors.
